newsitem.title: HAITI: Public transit strike slows Haitian capital.
newsitem.headline: Public transit strike slows Haitian capital.

text.p: The normally traffic-clogged streets of Haiti's capital were almost empty on Tuesday on the first day of a strike by public transit drivers protesting a recent rise in gasoline prices.

Drivers of taxis, public buses and tap-taps -- the colourfully decorated jitneys that throng the streets of Port-au-Prince -- struck to protest a tax that took the price of a gallon of gasoline from about $2 to $2.33.
"The price of gas has increased three times this year and the fare has not, so we can't even buy parts for our cars," said Raymond Cineus, a 26-year-old public transit driver.
Drivers who worked on Tuesday were threatened by strikers who said they would throw stones at public transit vehicles if they passed through City Soleil, the city's largest slum.
Radio reports said business had been slowed by the strike, with many Haitians unable to get to work.

Drivers said the strike would continue until the price of gas is lowered. But the government, which negotiatiated all day on Monday with union leaders, said the tax was the result of an increase in gas prices on the international market and lifting it was not an option.

"The government is willing to negotiate with the strikers, but it is not possible to lower the price on gas. The only option is to raise the fare for passengers," Minister of Commerce Fresnel Germain told Haitian radio.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, has struggled to revive its economy since the restoration of democratic rule in 1994. Rising food prices have left many Haitians unable to afford the barest of necessities.
"It's not a regulated raise in fare we want, because Haitians can't afford it," said taxi driver William Fils-Aime.
In the past few months Haiti's fledgling democracy has been plagued by a wave of debilitating strikes.
